entities.name: Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk (APK, Afrikaans Protestant Church), founded in 1987 as a breakaway from the Nederduits Gereformeerde Kerk (Dutch Reformed Church, DRC) — was established by a minority faction that rejected the DRC's 1986 decision to declare apartheid a sin and to open its congregations to all races, representing the extreme theological right-wing of Afrikaner Christianity that maintained the 19th-century Dutch Reformed theological justification for racial separation.

The APK's founding in 1987 — just as apartheid was beginning to face increasing international pressure and internal resistance — reflected the divisions within Afrikaner society between those who recognized apartheid as unjust and those who maintained it as God-ordained. The Dutch Reformed Church's role in providing theological legitimacy to apartheid (a role the DRC itself has subsequently repented and confessed as sinful) was central to apartheid's cultural foundation; when the DRC began to reverse this position, conservatives broke away.

The APK remains a small denomination whose founding represents the extreme theological position that racial separation is divinely mandated — a position now widely condemned as incompatible with Christian ethics. The church's existence is a historical monument to the theological extremity of apartheid justification and a reminder that the DRC's apartheid theology had true believers even as the apartheid system was collapsing.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk — founded in 1987 to maintain apartheid theology after the Dutch Reformed Church renounced it — is historically significant as a monument to the extreme theological justification of racial separation and the Afrikaner Christian nationalism that undergirded apartheid.
